# Switzerland — Builder Mode

Builder-mode derivation constraint: builder-mode content derives strictly from `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, `metadata.md`, and `profile.md`.

This file translates the normalized Switzerland profile into builder-facing interpretation.

This file provides structural interpretation only. It does not assign routing authority, readiness tiers, Atlas surfaces, jurisdiction rankings, or deployment suitability.

## Crypto-Legal Infrastructure Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a statutory supervision environment for regulated DLT trading venues where documented FINMA licensing rules, Swiss-law entity requirements, SDX continuity, BX Digital licensing, and Project Helvetia Phase III activity place legacy and tokenized settlement environments in the same supervised setting. The current normalized layers support reading Switzerland as a supervisory-stability context for digital-asset infrastructure licensing and wholesale CBDC experimentation continuity without characterizing the jurisdiction as permissive or experimentally open-ended.

## Multilateral Financial Governance Hosting Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a hosting environment for multilateral financial-governance institutional presence centered on Basel. The current normalized layers show BIS headquarters presence, Basel Committee hosting continuity through the BIS, and Financial Stability Board secretariat continuity in Basel. These conditions support a reading of Switzerland as a venue environment for prudential coordination dialogue and financial-governance institutional hosting without assigning coordination authority.

## Research and Scientific Compute Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a distributed institutional AI research environment with national-scale scientific compute availability. The current normalized layers show ETH AI Center participation, EPFL participation, Swiss National AI Institute coordination, and CSCS Alps operation as a national-scale compute and data research infrastructure. They also preserve a multisite research-compute continuity topology across Lugano, Lausanne, Villigen, and Bologna. This supports a builder-facing reading centered on distributed institutional research participation and scientific-compute continuity rather than frontier-compute designation.

## Transmission Interoperability Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a continental transmission interoperability participant with visible cross-border electricity coordination continuity. The current normalized layers show Swissgrid ownership of the national high-voltage transmission network, balancing responsibility, dense measurement visibility, and coordination with European partners because electricity flows cross national borders. This supports a builder-facing reading centered on interoperability participation, real-time grid-balancing continuity, and cross-border electricity-system coordination without assigning routing authority or energy-anchor classification.

## Neutral Exchange Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a carrier-neutral exchange infrastructure environment with local traffic-retention continuity. The current normalized layers show SwissIX non-profit exchange structure, neutral governance for internet-traffic exchange, and documented emphasis on local-resource use with reduced reliance on more distant global transit paths. This supports a builder-facing reading centered on neutral interconnection governance and exchange-layer continuity without assigning routing-core status.

## Trans-Alpine Logistics Interaction Surface

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a north-south rail-freight continuity environment shaped by base-tunnel modernization and trans-Alpine infrastructure stabilization. The current normalized layers show the NRLA system, including the Gotthard, Lötschberg, and Ceneri base tunnels, together with 4-metre freight-corridor modernization and SBB infrastructure backbone functions connecting manufacturers and logistics centres to the rail network. These conditions support a builder-facing reading centered on rail-throughput continuity and Alpine freight modernization without assigning logistics-hub classification.

## Governance Interaction Context

For builder interpretation, Switzerland reads as a Confederation-canton-commune distributed governance environment with a consensus executive structure and distributed supervisory authority layers. The current normalized layers show a three-level federal system, powers held close to communes and delegated upward when necessary, direct-democracy mechanisms across political levels, and a seven-member Federal Council whose decisions are made by consensus. This supports a builder-facing reading centered on distributed governance continuity rather than centralized national governance classification.

## Structural Boundary Conditions

The current Switzerland builder-mode reading also carries clear structural boundary conditions. The normalized layers do not support nationwide hyperscale compute concentration, semiconductor fabrication concentration, supranational legislative-alignment authority, or centralized national governance uniformity. Builder-facing interpretation therefore remains grounded in supervised digital-asset infrastructure, multilateral financial-governance hosting, distributed research-compute participation, transmission interoperability, neutral exchange continuity, and trans-Alpine freight systems rather than in absent concentration or authority conditions.

This file should be read as builder-facing interpretation of Switzerland's current structural posture within the normalized Atlas package only.

Builder-mode completeness status: high

Surface assignment status: none

# Switzerland — Profile

Profile derivation constraint: profile content derives strictly from `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, and `metadata.md`.

This file records the normalized Switzerland jurisdiction profile inside the Atlas global jurisdiction package.

Profile is the characterization layer of the package.

## Jurisdiction Overview

Switzerland currently reads within Atlas as a federal confederation with cantonal institutional distribution positioned inside the Alpine Crypto-Legal Corridor. The current package shows a statutory digital-asset infrastructure supervision environment, a documented host setting for multilateral financial-governance institutions in Basel, a distributed scientific-compute and AI research environment, a cross-border transmission interoperability environment, a neutral exchange-layer infrastructure environment, and a trans-Alpine freight continuity environment. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on crypto-legal infrastructure governance continuity, multilateral hosting stability, distributed research-compute participation, exchange neutrality, and Alpine logistics continuity without assigning coordination authority or topology control status.

## Crypto-Legal Infrastructure Environment

Switzerland's crypto-legal infrastructure environment is characterized in the current package by documented statutory accommodation for regulated DLT trading facilities and documented supervisory continuity around digital-asset market infrastructure. The current package shows FINMA licensing rules for DLT trading facilities, Swiss-law entity requirements for those facilities, documented approval of SIX Digital Exchange, documented licensing of BX Digital, and documented Project Helvetia Phase III settlement experimentation in a Swiss-franc wholesale central-bank-digital-currency context. These conditions support a structural characterization in which established financial-market supervision and tokenized-settlement experimentation are both present in the same national environment, without characterizing Switzerland as an unrestricted or permissive crypto jurisdiction.

## International Financial Governance Hosting Role

Switzerland's international financial-governance hosting role is characterized in the current package by documented Basel-based institutional concentration. The current package shows the Bank for International Settlements head office in Basel, Basel Committee activity through the BIS as a forum for banking-supervisory cooperation, and Financial Stability Board secretariat presence in Basel hosted by the BIS. These conditions support a structural characterization of Switzerland as a venue for prudential coordination dialogue and financial-stability secretariat continuity without assigning global coordination authority.

## Research and Scientific Compute Environment

Switzerland's research and scientific compute environment is characterized in the current package by distributed institutional participation and national-scale compute availability. The current package shows ETH AI Center participation, EPFL participation in the Swiss AI Initiative and Swiss National AI Institute, Swiss National AI Institute coordination of national-level trustworthy and open AI activity, and CSCS Alps operation as a national-scale general-purpose compute and data research infrastructure. The package also preserves multisite research-compute continuity across Lugano, Lausanne, Villigen, and Bologna. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on distributed institutional research topology and scientific-compute continuity rather than frontier-compute classification.

## Energy and Transmission Interoperability Environment

Switzerland's energy and transmission interoperability environment is characterized in the current package by high-voltage national transmission continuity and cross-border coordination. The current package shows Swissgrid ownership of the Swiss transmission grid, national high-voltage infrastructure, documented balancing responsibility, dense monitoring and measurement visibility, and coordination with European partners because electricity flows cross national borders. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on continental transmission interoperability participation and cross-border electricity-system continuity. The current package remains transmission-focused and does not extend to a fuller generation-source or continental routing-authority characterization.

## Neutral Connectivity Exchange Environment

Switzerland's neutral connectivity exchange environment is characterized in the current package by documented exchange neutrality and local interconnection continuity. The current package shows SwissIX as a non-profit exchange structure, neutral infrastructure for internet-traffic exchange in Switzerland, and support for local-resource use with reduced reliance on more distant global transit paths. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on carrier-neutral interconnection continuity and local traffic-retention infrastructure without assigning routing-core status.

## Trans-Alpine Logistics Continuity Role

Switzerland's trans-Alpine logistics continuity role is characterized in the current package by rail-freight modernization and north-south corridor persistence. The current package shows the NRLA tunnel system, including the Gotthard, Lötschberg, and Ceneri base tunnels, together with 4-metre freight-corridor modernization and SBB infrastructure backbone functions linking manufacturers and logistics centres to the rail network. The package also preserves documented freight-train throughput continuity on the Gotthard corridor after the base-tunnel timetable change. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on trans-Alpine freight continuity and north-south rail modernization rather than logistics-hub designation.

## Governance Structure Context

Switzerland's governance structure context is characterized in the current package by Confederation, canton, and commune distribution together with a consensus executive model. The current package shows a federal system operating across three political levels, powers held as close as possible to communes and delegated upward when necessary, direct-democracy mechanisms at different political levels, and a seven-member Federal Council whose decisions are made by consensus. These conditions support a structural characterization centered on distributed governance and supervisory continuity rather than centralized national governance classification.

## Structural Boundary Conditions

The current Switzerland profile also carries clear structural boundary conditions. The current package does not preserve nationwide hyperscale compute concentration, semiconductor fabrication concentration, supranational legislative-alignment authority, or centralized national governance uniformity. Current continuity is instead grounded in supervised digital-asset infrastructure, multilateral financial-governance hosting, distributed research-compute participation, transmission interoperability, neutral exchange infrastructure, and trans-Alpine freight systems. These boundary conditions remain descriptive and do not modify the corridor placement recorded in `metadata.md`.

This profile does not assign routing authority, topology completion control, readiness tiers, Atlas surfaces, jurisdiction rankings, or deployment suitability.

Profile completeness status: high

evidence.content:
# Switzerland — Evidence Layer

## Scope

This file records only country-level structural anchors documented for Switzerland that are sufficient to support later Atlas signal derivation.

It does not perform a complete canton-by-canton infrastructure survey and does not assign trust posture, routing role, coordination tier, investment rank, or Atlas surfaces.

## Federal governance and cantonal distribution

Switzerland has documented multi-level federal governance distributed across the Confederation, cantons, and communes.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- a federal system operating across three political levels: the Confederation, the cantons, and the communes
- a documented count of 26 cantons within the Swiss federal structure
- direct-democracy mechanisms that allow citizens to vote on specific issues at different political levels
- a governance model that keeps powers as close as possible to communes and delegates powers upward only when necessary
- a seven-member Federal Council operating as a collegial executive body whose decisions are made by consensus

These materials document a distributed governance environment with formal subnational variation and consensus-oriented federal structure.

### Canonical sources

- About Switzerland, "Political system" — https://www.aboutswitzerland.eda.admin.ch/en/political-system
- About Switzerland, "Federalism" — https://www.aboutswitzerland.eda.admin.ch/en/federalism

## Data-protection and information-governance framework

Switzerland has documented national privacy legislation and an independent federal supervisory authority for data protection and freedom of information.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- the new Federal Act on Data Protection taking effect for Swiss companies from 1 September 2023
- legislative updates that improved the processing of personal data and granted new rights to affected persons
- explicit inclusion of privacy-by-design and privacy-by-default principles in the current implementation guidance
- treatment of genetic and biometric data as sensitive data in the current implementation guidance
- the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner as an independent authority responsible for data protection and freedom-of-information matters
- the FDPIC role in supervising whether federal bodies and private companies process personal data lawfully
- the FDPIC role in mediating access-to-document disputes under the Freedom of Information Act
- explicit FDPIC guidance that the Federal Data Protection Act is directly applicable to AI-supported data processing

These materials document an active federal privacy and information-governance framework rather than an absence of regulatory structure.

### Canonical sources

- KMU Portal, "New Federal Act on Data Protection (nFADP)" — https://www.kmu.admin.ch/kmu/en/home/facts-and-trends/digitization/data-protection/new-federal-act-on-data-protection-nfadp.html
- Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner — https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en

## Regulated digital-asset and financial-market infrastructure environment

Switzerland has documented legal and supervisory structures for distributed-ledger-based financial-market activity.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- a FINMA licensing regime for DLT trading facilities under Article 73a ff. and related provisions
- a requirement that a DLT trading facility be structured as a legal entity under Swiss law with its registered office and head office in Switzerland
- FINMA responsibility for licensing, supervision, and change approvals for DLT trading facilities
- the DLT Act entering into force in Switzerland on 1 August 2021 as the legal basis for the new market-infrastructure category
- FINMA licensing of BX Digital as the first DLT trading facility in Switzerland in 2025
- FINMA documentation that the DLT framework supports innovation without compromising stability and security for market participants
- SIX Digital Exchange approval to operate integrated trading, settlement, and custody infrastructure for digital securities in a fully regulated environment
- continued digital-bond issuance activity on SDX exceeding CHF 1 billion on-platform by 2024
- Project Helvetia Phase III settlement activity in Swiss-franc wholesale central-bank digital currency within the current SDX source set

These materials document a regulated digital-asset market-infrastructure environment with visible supervisory and exchange-layer implementation.

### Canonical sources

- FINMA, "Licensing as a DLT trading facility" — https://www.finma.ch/en/authorisation/fintech/dlt-handelssystem/
- FINMA, "FINMA licenses first DLT trading facility" — https://www.finma.ch/en/news/2025/03/20250318-mm-dlt-handelssystem/
- SIX, "SIX Digital Exchange gets regulatory approval from FINMA" — https://www.six-group.com/en/newsroom/media-releases/2021/20210910-sdx-finma-approval.html
- SIX, "SIX Digital Exchange hits Milestone with over 1 Billion Swiss Francs in Digital Assets on their platform" — https://www.six-group.com/en/newsroom/media-releases/2024/20240521-six-sdx-digital-bonds-milestone.html

## International Financial Governance Hosting

Switzerland has documented hosting presence for major international monetary and financial-governance institutions, especially in Basel.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- the Bank for International Settlements having its head office in Basel, Switzerland
- BIS headquarters operations at Centralbahnplatz 2 in Basel
- the BIS role as an institution owned by 63 central banks representing economies accounting for about 95% of world GDP
- the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision operating through the BIS as the primary global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks
- the Basel Committee providing a forum for regular cooperation on banking supervisory matters across 45 members from 28 jurisdictions
- the Financial Stability Board being established as a not-for-profit association under Swiss law
- the Financial Stability Board Secretariat being located in Basel, Switzerland and hosted by the BIS
- formal concentration in Basel of international standard-setting and financial-stability coordination functions rather than only domestic Swiss banking institutions

These materials document international institutional hosting and financial-governance concentration in Basel without assigning routing authority or topology interpretation.

### Canonical sources

- BIS, "About BIS - overview" — https://www.bis.org/about/index.htm
- BIS, "Contact" — https://www.bis.org/about/contact.htm
- BIS, "The Basel Committee - overview" — https://www.bis.org/bcbs/index.htm
- Financial Stability Board, "Organisational Structure and Governance" — https://www.fsb.org/about/organisation-and-governance/
- Financial Stability Board, "Contact" — https://www.fsb.org/about/contact/

## National transmission-grid backbone and cross-border electricity coordination

Switzerland has documented national transmission-grid ownership and real-time operating visibility through Swissgrid.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- Swissgrid ownership of the Swiss transmission grid
- a transmission network of more than 6,700 kilometres operating at 380 and 220 kilovolts
- a documented footprint of 147 substations within the transmission-grid layer
- Swissgrid responsibility for regular maintenance, upgrades, and appropriate expansions to keep the grid available
- real-time operational monitoring across around 40,000 metering points and roughly 10,000 measured values processed within seconds
- explicit Swissgrid responsibility for balancing supply and demand around the clock
- documented coordination with European partners because electricity flows cross national borders

These materials document a nationally operated grid backbone with cross-border electricity coordination rather than an isolated domestic-only grid structure.

### Canonical sources

- Swissgrid, "The path of electricity through the Swiss transmission grid" — https://www.swissgrid.ch/en/home/operation/power-grid/swiss-power-grid.html
- Swissgrid, "Current grid key figures" — https://www.swissgrid.ch/en/home/operation/grid-data/current-data.html

## Rail, freight, and transalpine corridor infrastructure

Switzerland has documented dense rail infrastructure and transalpine freight programs tied to national and cross-border logistics.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- SBB Infrastructure describing itself as the backbone of Switzerland with operational control of the railways
- around 10,000 SBB Infrastructure staff supporting daily passenger and goods movement
- SBB company reporting daily transport volumes above one million passengers and substantial daily freight tonnage
- around 600 sidings connecting manufacturers and logistics centres directly to the SBB rail network
- SBB reporting that almost 90% of conventional rail goods transport uses these sidings
- Federal Office of Transport documentation that the New Rail Link through the Alps comprises the Gotthard, Lötschberg, and Ceneri base tunnels
- federal documentation that the NRLA shortens travel times and promotes rail freight
- federal documentation that Switzerland built the NRLA and 4-metre corridor to allow more freight trains to travel under easier conditions on the Gotthard route
- SBB reporting that, after the Gotthard Base Tunnel timetable change, up to four freight trains per hour in each direction could operate and that the tunnel marked a major step toward a flat rail route through the Alps for international transit traffic

These materials document strong rail-logistics continuity and transalpine freight-corridor relevance in the current source set.

### Canonical sources

- SBB Company — https://company.sbb.ch/en/home.html
- SBB, "Infrastructure" — https://company.sbb.ch/en/company/about-us/organisation/infrastructure.html
- Federal Office of Transport, "The New Rail Link through the Alps (NRLA)" — https://www.bav.admin.ch/en/nrla-new-rail-link-through-the-alps
- Federal Office of Transport, "Transfer of transalpine freight traffic from road to rail" — https://www.bav.admin.ch/bav/en/home/modes-of-transport/railways/freight-transport/transfer-from-road-to-rail.html
- SBB, "Freight traffic is becoming more efficient and more environment-friendly" — https://company.sbb.ch/en/the-company/projects/mittelland-region-and-the-ticino/neat/freight-services.html

## Internet-exchange and local interconnection presence

Switzerland has documented neutral internet-exchange infrastructure for local traffic exchange.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- SwissIX describing itself as the largest Internet Exchange Point in Switzerland in terms of port capacity and bandwidth
- SwissIX operating as a non-profit association
- SwissIX historical formation by Swiss internet service providers to create neutral infrastructure for exchanging internet traffic in Switzerland
- SwissIX documentation that local exchange of traffic reduces reliance on more distant global transit paths and encourages use of local resources

These materials document local interconnection presence and neutral exchange infrastructure without establishing a broader European backbone or routing-dominance claim.

### Canonical sources

- SwissIX — https://www.swissix.ch/
- SwissIX, "About" — https://www.swissix.ch/about/
- SwissIX, "What is an Internet Exchange Point (IXP)" — https://www.swissix.ch/about/what-is-an-ixp/

## Research, AI, and high-performance compute infrastructure

Switzerland has documented nationally visible AI, research, and high-performance compute infrastructure anchored by ETH Zurich, EPFL, and CSCS.

The current Switzerland package preserves evidence of:

- the ETH AI Center serving as ETH Zurich's central hub for artificial intelligence across foundations, applications, and implications
- the Swiss AI Initiative as a large open-science and open-source effort for AI foundation models launched through the ETH AI Center and EPFL AI Center partnership
- the Swiss National AI Institute launched by ETH Zurich and EPFL to steer national-level research, education, and innovation in trustworthy and open AI
- Swiss National AI Institute plans for a national foundation model supported by supercomputer infrastructure of more than 10,000 next-generation AI GPUs
- CSCS Alps operating as a general-purpose compute and data research infrastructure open to researchers in Switzerland and internationally
- Alps support for dedicated virtual clusters including weather forecasting, user-lab work, and machine-learning and AI workloads
